text: Jerry John Rawlings (22 June 1947 – 12 November 2020) was a Ghanaian military officer, aviator, and politician who led the country briefly in 1979 and then from 1981 to 2001. He ruled through a military regime until 1993 and then served two terms as democratically elected president of Ghana, making him the longest-serving leader in Ghana's history, presiding over the nation for 19 years. Rawlings came to power as a flight lieutenant in the Ghana Air Force following a coup on 15 May 1979, after an earlier failed coup attempt on the same date, five weeks before scheduled democratic elections. He was arrested and sentenced to death by a General Court Martial for his role in the 1979 coup but was released on 4 June 1979 by a group of soldiers who then overthrew the government of General Fred Akuffo. He established the Armed Forces Revolutionary Council (AFRC) and ruled for 112 days, during which he ordered the execution of eight military officers and three former heads of state. Power was peacefully handed over to President Hilla Limann on 24 September 1979. On 31 December 1981, Rawlings led a second coup, overthrowing Limann and establishing the Provisional National Defence Council (PNDC) military junta, citing weak civilian rule and economic decline. During this period, he ordered the secret abduction and killing of Supreme Court justices Cecilia Koranteng-Addow, Frederick Sarkodie, and Kwadjo Agyei Agyepong, as well as military officers Major Sam Acquah and Major Dasana Nantogmah; Joachim Amartey Kwei and four others were convicted and executed in 1982, with Corporal Amedaka escaping. The PNDC implemented strict economic policies, including a state monopoly on trade, price controls, and the destruction of the Makola No.1 Market, which led to economic crisis by 1983 and forced structural adjustment. In 1992, Rawlings resigned from the military, founded the National Democratic Congress (NDC), and won the presidential election with 60% of the vote, defeating Professor Adu Boahen (31%), Hilla Limann (6.8%), Kwabena Darko (2.9%), and Emmanuel Erskine (1.7%), with a 50% voter turnout. His victory was aided by the "organs of the revolution," including Committees for the Defence of the Revolution, Commando Units, and the 31 December Women's Organization, and by state control of media through PNDC Law 221 and a 20,000 Cedis campaign contribution cap. The Commonwealth Observer Group declared the election "free and fair," though the International Foundation for Electoral Systems noted possible errors in voter registration. Opposition parties boycotted subsequent elections, leading to a one-party parliament with NDC winning 189 of 200 seats. The PNDC was transformed into the NDC. Rawlings took office on 7 January 1993, marking the beginning of the Fourth Republic. He implemented the Economic Recovery Program (ERP) in 1982, which included currency devaluation, removal of price controls, social-service subsidies favoring farmers, privatization of state enterprises, and reduced government spending, supported by $800 million from 1987–1988 and $900 million in 1989. Between 1992 and 1996, he eased control over the judiciary and civil society, allowing an independent Supreme Court and independent newspapers. The 1996 election saw improved oversight, with nearly 9.2 million voters registered at 19,000 polling stations, the establishment of the Network of Domestic Election Observers (NEDEO), over 60,000 candidate agents monitoring polling sites, and a parallel vote-tabulation system. The Inter-Party Advisory Committee (IPAC) was formed to manage election preparations and complaints. The election was peaceful with a 78% turnout, and Rawlings won 57% to John Kufuor’s 40%. The NDC secured 134 seats in the Assembly, while the opposition won 66 and the NPP won 60. The 1992 constitution limits a president to two terms, and Rawlings did not seek a third term in 2000. He retired in 2001 and was succeeded by John Kufuor, his main rival in 1996. Kufuor won the 2000 presidential election after defeating Rawlings' vice-president John Atta Mills in a runoff, and Mills conceded to Kufuor in 2004. In November 2000, Rawlings was named the first International Year of Volunteers 2001 Eminent Person by UN Secretary-General Kofi Annan. In October 2010, he was appointed African Union envoy to Somalia and attended Dési Bouterse’s inauguration in Suriname, where he explored Ghanaian ties to the Maroon people. He delivered lectures at universities, including Oxford University, and in July 2019 led a three-day working trip to Burkina Faso as Chairman of the Thomas Sankara Memorial Committee. In September 2019, he led Ghana’s delegation to Robert Mugabe’s funeral. Rawlings died on 12 November 2020 at Korle-Bu Teaching Hospital in Accra, a week after being admitted for a "short term illness," with some reports indicating complications as the cause of death.

Jerry John Rawlings, a prominent Ghanaian political figure, was recognized by UN Secretary-General Kofi Annan as a "minent Person" and actively participated in various events and conferences to promote volunteerism. In October 2010, he was appointed African Union envoy to Somalia. In November 2010, he attended the inauguration of Dési Bouterse as President of Suriname and toured the country, showing particular interest in the Ghanaian origins of the Maroon people. Rawlings delivered lectures at universities, including Oxford University in England, and maintained strong support for the National Democratic Congress (NDC). In July 2019, he undertook a three-day working trip to Burkina Faso as Chairman of the Thomas Sankara Memorial Committee. In September 2019, he led the Ghanaian governmental delegation to the funeral of Robert Mugabe, the late former president of Zimbabwe. Rawlings died on 12 November 2020 at Korle-Bu Teaching Hospital in Accra, a week after being admitted for a "short term illness"; according to some reports, his death was due to complications from COVID-19. His death occurred nearly two months after that of his mother, Victoria Agbotui, who passed away on 24 September 2020. President Nana Akufo-Addo declared a seven-day period of mourning, with flags flown at half-mast, and his family appealed to the Government of Ghana to bury him in Keta in the Volta Region. A schedule for signing a book of condolence was opened in his memory, and his funeral, originally scheduled for 23 December 2020, was postponed at the family's request. From 24 to 27 January 2021, funeral ceremonies were held in Accra, including a requiem mass at the Holy Spirit Cathedral on 24 January 2021, followed by a vigil at the Air Force Officers' Mess later that evening. His body was laid in state in the foyer of the Accra International Conference Centre from 25 to 26 January 2021. Traditional rites were performed by the Anlo Ewe people of his maternal ancestry. On 27 January 2021, a state funeral attended by national and international political leaders, paramount chiefs, diplomats, and other dignitaries was held at Black Star Square, followed by a burial service at the Military Cemetery at Burma Camp, with full military honours, including a slow march by the cortège, a flypast by a Ghana Air Force helicopter, the sounding of the Last Post by army buglers, and a 21-gun salute. President Nana Akufo-Addo proposed to the Governing Council of UDS to rename the institution after Jerry Rawlings, who used his US$50,000 Hunger Project prize as seed money to establish the university, a suggestion accepted by his family. A foundation called the JJ Rawlings Foundation was established in his name and led by his children, Madam Yaa Asantewaa Agyeman-Rawlings and Madam Amina Agyeman-Rawlings. In May 2025, the government of Burkina Faso named a street in Ouagadougou after him, with signage reading "Avenue Flt Lt Jerry John Rawlings, Ancien President du Ghana, ne le 22/06/1947 - dcd le 12/11/2020"; the naming coincided with the unveiling of a monument in memory of his assassinated friend and former Burkinabe leader, Thomas Sankara. Physical books related to Jerry Rawlings are available for reference, including Shipley, Jesse Weaver.
